Give hyperosmolar agent (mannitol or hypertonic saline) according to paediatric DKA cerebral-injury protocol without awaiting CT.
Reassess fluids, insulin, electrolytes, glucose and ventilation; avoid unnecessary hyperventilation.
CT/MRI when stabilised to assess differential causes.
management.safety: Do not delay cerebral-injury treatment for imaging.
management.local: Paediatric doses, age thresholds and neonatal algorithms must be checked against local protocols and senior paediatric advice.

stem: A 34-year-old after a fall has a deformed forearm with a 4 cm wound communicating with visible bone. Distal pulse and sensation are present, BP stable. There is gravel contamination.
ask: Which treatment sequence is MOST appropriate?
options: Give IV antibiotics, cover the wound and arrange operative debridement.
Clean and close the open wound in ED after documenting distal pulses.
Give oral antibiotics and arrange delayed surgical review after swelling settles.
Delay antibiotics until deep operative cultures are obtained in theatre.
Perform CT angiography first because all open fractures injure major arteries.
explanations: Correct: infection prevention begins immediately, with definitive surgery guided by fracture and wound severity. Clinical distinction: Open fractures require early IV antibiotics, sterile coverage, neurovascular documentation and surgical source control.

Primary tight closure of a gravel-contaminated open fracture in ED risks trapping infection and misses necessary operative irrigation and debridement. Sterile coverage, IV antibiotics and urgent orthopaedic care are standard.
Oral antibiotics alone are insufficient for an open fracture with exposed bone and contamination. Prompt IV prophylaxis and operative debridement lower infection risk.

Operative samples may be obtained when indicated, but prophylactic IV antibiotics should be started as early as possible rather than delayed for cultures. Tetanus prophylaxis and wound management also matter.

Vascular imaging is indicated for absent pulses or signs of vascular injury, not automatically with intact perfusion and sensation. Initial antibiotics, sterile dressing, splinting and orthopaedic review should not be delayed.
pearl: Open fractures require early IV antibiotics, sterile coverage, neurovascular documentation and surgical source control.
pivot: If the fracture is CLOSED, stable, and neurovascularly intact: give analgesia, obtain the appropriate X-rays, align/splint or cast as indicated, document and recheck distal circulation/sensation, and arrange fracture-clinic review. Do NOT give routine open-fracture IV antibiotics or operative wound debridement; urgent orthopaedic review is still needed for vascular compromise, marked displacement or instability.

steps: Give IV antibiotics, cover the wound and arrange operative debridement.
Remove gross debris only when appropriate, saline-moistened sterile cover, immobilise and treat pain.
Prompt IV antibiotics selected for grade and contamination, tetanus assessment.
Urgent orthopaedic/plastic assessment for debridement and stabilisation.
management.safety: Do not repeatedly probe the open wound or perform unplanned closure.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 28-year-old is found unresponsive with RR 5/min, pinpoint pupils and SpO2 75%. A syringe is nearby. A pulse is present; he responds only to painful stimulus.
ask: Which is the BEST immediate treatment?
options: Give low-dose naloxone alone without supporting respiratory ventilation.
Perform rapid toxicology screening before administering any opioid reversal.
Give IV flumazenil first because pinpoint pupils indicate sedative ingestion.
Support airway ventilation now and titrate naloxone to reverse dangerous opioid hypoventilation.
Use a sedative drug for agitation before correcting oxygenation or ventilation.
explanations: Naloxone is crucial, but with RR 5/min and SpO2 75%, provide immediate airway positioning and assisted ventilation while giving and titrating reversal. Antidote alone may not act quickly enough.
Urine toxicology cannot reliably guide emergency airway management and may be delayed or misleading. The toxidrome and hypoventilation justify immediate naloxone and ventilation.

Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines in selected circumstances, not opioids, and can precipitate seizures in mixed overdoses. Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression point toward an opioid toxidrome.

Correct: ventilation is vital; naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression but may wear off before the opioid. Clinical distinction: In opioid overdose the target is adequate ventilation, not forcing complete alertness at the cost of severe withdrawal.
Sedation worsens respiratory depression and can cause arrest in an already profoundly hypoxaemic patient. The initial priorities are breathing support and opioid reversal.
pearl: In opioid overdose the target is adequate ventilation, not forcing complete alertness at the cost of severe withdrawal.
pivot: If pulseless, initiate CPR and advanced life support while treating likely opioid cause.

steps: Support airway ventilation now and titrate naloxone to reverse dangerous opioid hypoventilation.
Titrated naloxone IV/IM/intranasal per local pathway; repeat or infuse for long-acting opioids.
Watch for re-sedation, aspiration, pulmonary complications and precipitated withdrawal.
Offer overdose education, take-home naloxone and addiction support after recovery.
management.safety: Do not leave a patient unobserved once naloxone initially works.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 69-year-old experiences 12 minutes of left arm weakness and speech slurring, now completely resolved. BP 150/90 mmHg, irregularly irregular pulse 104/min and glucose normal. He has no headache or prior stroke.
ask: What is the BEST next step?
options: Start aspirin and defer vascular imaging if weakness has completely resolved.
Give therapeutic anticoagulation immediately without excluding haemorrhage.
Arrange same-day TIA assessment, brain imaging and secondary prevention.
Arrange outpatient EEG first to exclude focal seizure as the primary cause.
Schedule neurological review in several weeks because the episode was brief.
explanations: Transient symptom resolution is typical for TIA and does not remove early stroke risk. Urgent imaging, vascular and cardiac assessment, plus antithrombotic decisions are needed.

AF raises embolic risk and anticoagulation may be indicated after assessment, but timing and agent choice depend on imaging, stroke/TIA evaluation and bleeding considerations. Do not start empirically before appropriate workup.

Correct: expedite aetiology and secondary prevention; atrial fibrillation is a possible cardioembolic source. Clinical distinction: Resolved focal deficit is a TIA emergency: evaluate rapidly and intervene on stroke mechanisms.
Focal seizure can occasionally mimic TIA, but a sudden negative deficit with speech disturbance and vascular risk deserves urgent cerebrovascular assessment. EEG is not the first priority.
The first hours to days after TIA carry meaningful stroke risk. Same-day specialist assessment and prevention are more appropriate than routine follow-up.
pearl: Resolved focal deficit is a TIA emergency: evaluate rapidly and intervene on stroke mechanisms.
pivot: If MRI shows infarction, the event is tissue-positive stroke even if symptoms have resolved.

steps: Arrange same-day TIA assessment, brain imaging and secondary prevention.
Brain and vascular imaging per protocol, ECG for AF, BP, lipids, glucose and carotid disease.
Antiplatelet or anticoagulation according to mechanism/timing, statin and risk-factor management.
Return immediately for recurrent symptoms; driving and lifestyle guidance.
management.safety: Do not delay referral based solely on a low risk score.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 64-year-old is brought to the ED 50 minutes after sudden right-arm weakness and expressive aphasia. Blood glucose is 5.6 mmol/L. BP 174/92 mmHg and NIHSS is 12. He has no head injury.
ask: What is the BEST next investigation/action sequence?
options: Give aspirin immediately and organise CT if deficits persist after observation.
Arrange MRI with contrast before contacting the acute stroke team.
Obtain emergency brain CT and vascular imaging through the stroke pathway.
Begin IV thrombolysis before CT because he is within the treatment window.
Order carotid duplex as the only urgent investigation for unilateral weakness.
explanations: Aspirin can be appropriate after haemorrhage is excluded and a reperfusion decision is made. Observing ongoing disabling aphasia before imaging wastes a narrow treatment window.
MRI can be valuable in stroke diagnosis, but routine contrast MRI before acute stroke activation may delay rapid non-contrast CT, vascular imaging and reperfusion assessment.

Correct: exclude haemorrhage immediately and assess IV thrombolysis and large-vessel thrombectomy eligibility within time windows. Clinical distinction: Stroke treatments depend on time, imaging, premorbid function and contraindications; normal glucose helps exclude a mimic, not haemorrhage.
Thrombolysis eligibility depends on excluding intracranial haemorrhage and assessing contraindications. Treating before emergent brain imaging risks fatal bleeding.
Carotid ultrasound may be part of secondary evaluation but does not exclude haemorrhage, identify intracranial large-vessel occlusion or guide the entire acute reperfusion pathway.
pearl: Stroke treatments depend on time, imaging, premorbid function and contraindications; normal glucose helps exclude a mimic, not haemorrhage.
pivot: If symptoms have completely resolved, assess as TIA with urgent vascular/cardiac risk evaluation rather than dismissing the episode.

steps: Obtain emergency brain CT and vascular imaging through the stroke pathway.
Immediate non-contrast CT to exclude bleed and CT angiography when indicated to assess proximal occlusion.
Determine thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy eligibility with BP and bleeding-risk screening; avoid empiric antiplatelets before exclusion of haemorrhage.
Swallow screen before oral intake, monitor BP, glucose and neuro status; secondary prevention after imaging and definitive treatment.
management.safety: Do not delay imaging while waiting for routine labs unless a specific safety issue dictates.
management.local: Educational sequence only: verify drug doses, contraindications and escalation pathways with your current local protocol and supervising clinician.

stem: A 4-month-old has 3 days of coryza and cough, diffuse fine crackles, RR 66/min, moderate recession, SpO2 89% in room air and only 40% of usual feeds over 12 hours. No focal findings suggest bacterial pneumonia.
ask: Which is the BEST treatment plan?
options: Start routine salbutamol nebulisation and reassess feeding in the morning.
Begin systemic corticosteroids as first-line anti-inflammatory bronchiolitis care.
Give IV antibiotics for possible pneumonia despite diffuse findings and coryza.
Observe at home with repeat saturation if oral intake remains below half.
Admit for oxygen and feeding support in moderate-to-severe bronchiolitis.
explanations: Salbutamol does not consistently improve typical infant bronchiolitis and is not routine first-line care. SpO2 89%, moderate recession and poor feeding require hospital support.
Systemic corticosteroids are not routinely recommended for uncomplicated viral bronchiolitis. Oxygen, hydration and monitoring address the immediate problems.
Bacterial coinfection may change therapy if new focal signs or toxicity appear, but diffuse crackles with viral prodrome do not justify routine antibiotics without evidence.
Home observation is inappropriate with hypoxaemia and intake only 40% of normal. The infant needs monitored oxygen and assisted feeding or fluids.

Correct: the key interventions are oxygenation, adequate fluid intake and monitoring work of breathing. Clinical distinction: For bronchiolitis, supportive care is the treatment; escalating work of breathing, apnoea, exhaustion and poor feeding are danger signs.
pearl: For bronchiolitis, supportive care is the treatment; escalating work of breathing, apnoea, exhaustion and poor feeding are danger signs.
pivot: In an older child with recurrent wheeze and a clear response to bronchodilator, consider viral-triggered asthma instead.

steps: Admit for oxygen and feeding support in moderate-to-severe bronchiolitis.
Give oxygen as local threshold requires, nasal saline/gentle suction if obstructed, smaller feeds or NG/IV fluids if oral intake inadequate.
Observe saturation, feeding and fatigue; high-flow nasal support/critical-care review for persistent hypoxaemia or exhaustion.
management.safety: Avoid unnecessary chest imaging, bronchodilators, antibiotics and systemic steroids in routine bronchiolitis.
management.local: Use current maternity/paediatric local protocols, weight-based prescribing checks and senior supervision for doses and timing.

stem: A 21-year-old three hours after tibial shaft fracture fixation has escalating leg pain despite opioids. Toes are warm and pulses palpable. Passive extension of the toes causes severe pain; calf compartments feel tense.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Request compartment-pressure measurement before contacting orthopaedics.
Apply ice and high elevation because palpable pulses exclude ischaemia.
Arrange emergency CT angiography before considering limb surgery.
Remove external constriction, call orthopaedics and prepare emergency fasciotomy for compartment syndrome.
Give more opioids and review pain after the next scheduled neurovascular check.
explanations: Pressure measurement can assist equivocal cases, but the escalating pain on passive stretch and tense compartments are clinically compelling. Do not delay urgent surgical evaluation to obtain numbers.
Distal pulses may persist until late compartment syndrome; they do not exclude threatened muscle and nerves. Elevation far above heart level may reduce arterial perfusion.
CTA is reserved for suspected arterial injury and does not treat rising compartment pressure. Urgent release and fasciotomy assessment are time-sensitive.

Correct: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch after trauma are classic signs needing urgent decompression. Clinical distinction: Acute compartment syndrome is a clinical time-critical diagnosis; present pulses or normal skin colour do NOT rule it out.
Escalating analgesia without recognising disproportionate pain and passive-stretch pain masks a limb-threatening syndrome. Notify orthopaedics immediately.
pearl: Acute compartment syndrome is a clinical time-critical diagnosis; present pulses or normal skin colour do NOT rule it out.
pivot: If findings are equivocal in a sedated/unreliable patient, compartment pressure measurement may help, but must not delay treatment of obvious disease.

steps: Remove external constriction, call orthopaedics and prepare emergency fasciotomy for compartment syndrome.
Split dressings/cast, keep limb near heart level, give oxygen/support BP and analgesia without delay.
Emergency surgical fasciotomy and postoperative monitoring for rhabdomyolysis, renal injury and wound complications.
management.safety: Delay can cause irreversible myonecrosis and nerve injury within hours.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: An 80-year-old taking apixaban for AF presents with melaena, BP 86/48 mmHg, Hb 69 g/L and ongoing haematemesis. Last apixaban dose was five hours ago. He is confused and cool peripherally.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate immediate plan?
options: Stop apixaban, resuscitate and discuss reversal with urgent endoscopy.
Start IV vitamin K and delay endoscopy until INR normalises.
Give apixaban-specific reversal without activating haemorrhage resuscitation.
Continue anticoagulation and use IV PPI alone until bleeding settles.
Prepare non-urgent endoscopy after a week of oral iron and observation.
explanations: Correct: major DOAC-associated bleeding warrants haemodynamic resuscitation and targeted reversal consideration. Clinical distinction: In major DOAC bleeding, stop the drug, stabilise physiology, consider reversal for life-threatening haemorrhage and control the source.
Vitamin K reverses vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin, not apixaban. A life-threatening GI bleed requires resuscitation, urgent endoscopy and consideration of a DOAC reversal strategy.
A reversal agent may be appropriate in selected severe bleeding, but it does not substitute for airway and circulatory support, blood products when needed and urgent endoscopic source control.
Stroke prevention matters in AF but active life-threatening haematemesis takes priority. Temporarily withholding apixaban and assessing reversal are standard while stabilising the bleed.
Haemodynamic shock, Hb 69 g/L and ongoing bleeding need immediate ED resuscitation and intervention, not outpatient iron or delayed investigation.
pearl: In major DOAC bleeding, stop the drug, stabilise physiology, consider reversal for life-threatening haemorrhage and control the source.
pivot: For minor self-limited bleeding, temporary interruption without reversal may be sufficient depending on risk and timing.

steps: Stop apixaban, resuscitate and discuss reversal with urgent endoscopy.
Stop apixaban; senior haematology review for factor Xa inhibitor reversal (specific agent or PCC based on availability/indication).
Urgent therapeutic endoscopy when stabilised; PPI if suspected ulcer and other source-specific treatment.
Reassess thromboembolism risk and timing of resuming anticoagulation with specialists.
management.safety: Do not use vitamin K or protamine as routine apixaban reversal; document time of last dose and renal function.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 27-year-old has nausea, jaundice and ALT 1600 U/L after taking multiple cold remedies and analgesics. INR is 2.0 and she is becoming confused; bilirubin is 86 µmol/L. There is no known chronic liver disease.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Obtain an abdominal ultrasound first and arrange routine hepatology follow-up.
Use fresh frozen plasma routinely to normalise INR before specialist referral.
Wait for a paracetamol concentration before beginning antidote treatment.
Treat presumed viral hepatitis with corticosteroids as definitive first-line care.
Start N-acetylcysteine and refer urgently for acute liver failure care.
explanations: Imaging may form part of aetiology workup, but INR elevation plus new encephalopathy suggests acute liver failure and requires immediate specialist admission, monitoring and treatment.
FFP is used for active bleeding or necessary procedures, not routinely simply to correct INR, as it may obscure prognostic monitoring. Address cause and transplant-centre evaluation urgently.

Multiple cold preparations may contain paracetamol, and a late or staggered ingestion can produce serious injury despite a low measured level. Start NAC promptly in suspected paracetamol-related acute liver injury while testing.

Viral hepatitis belongs in the differential, but empirical steroids without diagnosis do not treat possible paracetamol toxicity or acute liver failure. Obtain history and virology in parallel with stabilisation.

Correct: encephalopathy plus coagulopathy in acute liver injury suggests acute liver failure and potential transplantation needs. Clinical distinction: Acute liver failure is encephalopathy with significant coagulopathy after acute hepatic injury, regardless of transaminase magnitude.
pearl: Acute liver failure is encephalopathy with significant coagulopathy after acute hepatic injury, regardless of transaminase magnitude.
pivot: Isolated raised ALT with preserved INR and normal cognition may be assessed less urgently depending on cause.

steps: Start N-acetylcysteine and refer urgently for acute liver failure care.
Start NAC when suspected paracetamol injury or as advised by liver/toxicology service; check drug formulations and total cumulative dose.
Viral, autoimmune, medication/toxicology testing and Doppler imaging while consulting hepatology.
Discuss transplant-centre transfer, manage hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema risk and organ dysfunction.
management.safety: Do not give sedatives indiscriminately or delay transplant-centre contact for full aetiological confirmation.
management.local: Educational guidance; check current hospital guidelines, prescribing references and senior advice for exact treatment details.

stem: A 29-year-old at 20 weeks has an asymptomatic midstream urine culture showing 10^5 CFU/mL group B streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy and a normal renal scan.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate plan?
options: Give intrapartum prophylaxis only because there are no urinary symptoms.
Treat GBS bacteriuria now and provide intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.
Give a single oral antibiotic dose now without later labour prophylaxis.
Repeat the urine culture in six weeks before deciding whether to treat.
Recommend elective induction at 37 weeks instead of antibiotic prophylaxis.
explanations: GBS bacteriuria at a significant count should be treated antenatally even without symptoms, and its presence also indicates intrapartum prophylaxis because it marks increased maternal colonisation.

Correct: significant GBS bacteriuria merits treatment and is an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis even if follow-up culture clears. Clinical distinction: Any GBS bacteriuria in pregnancy signals heavy colonisation and need for intrapartum prophylaxis; treat current ASB according to colony count and policy.
An adequate antibiotic course treats asymptomatic bacteriuria; a single arbitrary dose is insufficient. Labour prophylaxis remains indicated irrespective of repeat culture clearance.

Delaying treatment of significant asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy increases pyelonephritis and obstetric risks. Treat promptly with a pregnancy-appropriate antibiotic, considering sensitivities.
Delivery timing is not changed solely because of GBS bacteriuria. Antenatal treatment plus intrapartum prophylaxis address maternal urinary and neonatal infection risks.
pearl: Any GBS bacteriuria in pregnancy signals heavy colonisation and need for intrapartum prophylaxis; treat current ASB according to colony count and policy.
pivot: GBS detected only on a late rectovaginal swab with no UTI is managed by intrapartum prophylaxis rather than antepartum eradication.

steps: Treat GBS bacteriuria now and provide intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.
Give appropriate pregnancy-compatible antibiotic course and confirm urine clearance according to local protocol.
Document GBS bacteriuria prominently for labour prophylaxis.
Review recurrent UTI symptoms and renal risk.
management.safety: Follow local antimicrobial sensitivity because GBS macrolide/clindamycin resistance varies.
management.local: Exam-oriented summary: confirm exact obstetric medication, fetal monitoring and delivery thresholds with the local maternity pathway.

stem: A 3-year-old develops reduced urine output and pallor five days after bloody diarrhoea. Hb is 76 g/L, platelets 58 ×10^9/L and creatinine 190 µmol/L. Blood film has schistocytes. Coagulation profile is normal.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Start antibiotics to eradicate residual gut bacteria despite evolving HUS.
Admit for supportive paediatric renal management of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Use plasma exchange routinely because every schistocyte syndrome is TTP.
Give prophylactic platelet transfusions to correct the count before admission.
Begin high-dose steroids as sole treatment for presumed immune thrombocytopenia.
explanations: Antibiotics are not routinely used for suspected shiga-toxin diarrhoeal illness and may increase risk in some circumstances. Once HUS develops, careful renal, blood pressure and fluid management is key.

Correct: typical shiga-toxin HUS is primarily managed supportively while monitoring kidney failure and haemolysis. Clinical distinction: The triad of microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and AKI after bloody diarrhoea suggests typical HUS.

TTP is an important thrombotic microangiopathy but differs in typical context and ADAMTS13 pathology. A young child after bloody diarrhoea with AKI, haemolysis and thrombocytopenia strongly suggests STEC-HUS, usually managed supportively.

Platelet transfusion is generally reserved for significant bleeding or procedures; routine normalisation is not required and may exacerbate microvascular thrombosis. Specialist paediatric renal care takes priority.
Isolated immune thrombocytopenia does not explain schistocytes, anaemia and AKI. Steroid monotherapy misses the renal and microangiopathic syndrome.
pearl: The triad of microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and AKI after bloody diarrhoea suggests typical HUS.
pivot: Atypical complement-mediated HUS may require targeted complement inhibition after specialist investigation.

steps: Admit for supportive paediatric renal management of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Careful fluid/electrolyte balance, avoid nephrotoxins, manage hypertension and dialyse for indications.
Red-cell transfusion when symptomatic/severe; avoid routine platelet transfusion.
Serial FBC/creatinine and stool shiga-toxin testing when indicated.
management.safety: Monitor for hyperkalaemia, hypertensive encephalopathy and seizures.
management.local: Paediatric doses, age thresholds and neonatal algorithms must be checked against local protocols and senior paediatric advice.

stem: A 70-year-old with a knee replacement three months ago has rapidly increasing joint pain, swelling and temperature 38.4°C. CRP is 172 mg/L; ultrasound shows an effusion and radiograph reveals no fracture. He remains haemodynamically stable.
ask: Which is the BEST next step?
options: Start empiric antibiotics before any joint aspirate despite haemodynamic stability.
Use intra-articular steroids for aseptic loosening and reassess after 48 hours.
Order CT to confirm hardware alignment before involving orthopaedics.
Aspirate the prosthetic knee for synovial cultures and seek urgent orthopaedic infection assessment.
Treat with oral antibiotics and defer joint sampling until inflammation settles.
explanations: Antibiotics may be urgently necessary if unstable, but in a stable suspected prosthetic joint infection, aspiration for culture before antimicrobials increases diagnostic yield. Involve orthopaedics promptly.

Prosthetic joint infection can present without radiographic abnormality, and steroid injection into a potentially infected joint may cause harm. Exclude infection before considering anti-inflammatory injection.
Imaging can evaluate mechanical complications, but the high CRP, fever and acute effusion demand microbiological joint sampling and infection-focused review.

Correct: suspected prosthetic joint infection needs microbiological diagnosis and coordinated surgical/antibiotic strategy. Clinical distinction: Prosthetic joint infection differs from native septic arthritis because biofilm and implant retention/exchange strategies matter.
Short oral courses may partially suppress cultures without eradicating deep prosthetic infection. Early orthopaedic sampling and a tailored surgical–antibiotic strategy are more appropriate.
pearl: Prosthetic joint infection differs from native septic arthritis because biofilm and implant retention/exchange strategies matter.
pivot: If haemodynamically unstable/septic, start broad IV antibiotics promptly after feasible cultures without waiting for aspiration.

steps: Aspirate the prosthetic knee for synovial cultures and seek urgent orthopaedic infection assessment.
Blood cultures and aseptic joint aspiration for cell count, cultures and crystals when stable.
Specialist-directed IV antibiotics and debridement/implant-retention or revision strategy by onset/stability.
Monitor inflammatory response and prolonged organism-specific therapy.
management.safety: Avoid starting antibiotics before necessary cultures when stable, but never delay in shock.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A healthy 43-year-old without family history asks for annual mammograms after a friend was diagnosed with breast cancer. She has average baseline risk, no breast symptoms and lives in a country with a population screening start age above 43.
ask: Which response is MOST appropriate?
options: Recommend annual MRI because a friend’s diagnosis independently raises her risk.
Offer mammography immediately without discussing possible false-positive results.
Refuse imaging requests categorically because she is below programme age.
Discuss individual screening benefits, harms and patient preferences.
Order blood tumour markers because they are safer than mammography.
explanations: Personal acquaintance with breast cancer does not by itself confer high hereditary risk; MRI is usually reserved for defined higher-risk circumstances. Clarify family history and objective risk first.
Imaging can be considered in some circumstances, but average-risk younger screening involves tradeoffs including false positives and overdiagnosis. Shared decision-making should precede testing.
She deserves a respectful informed discussion even when routine population invitations begin later. Explain baseline risk, symptom vigilance and when screening becomes routinely offered.

Correct: screening decisions should reflect evidence, age/risk and informed patient preference. Clinical distinction: Population screening depends on net benefit in an age/risk group; earlier testing can increase harms without comparable benefit.
Serum tumour markers are not validated population screening tests for asymptomatic average-risk breast cancer and may cause unnecessary investigation without reliable benefit.
pearl: Population screening depends on net benefit in an age/risk group; earlier testing can increase harms without comparable benefit.
pivot: A pathogenic high-risk mutation or strong pedigree requires formal risk assessment and earlier tailored surveillance.

steps: Discuss individual screening benefits, harms and patient preferences.
Absolute potential benefits, false positives, unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis; compare local screening intervals.
Shared plan and breast-awareness advice, with diagnostic imaging if new symptoms appear.
Review eligibility and preferences as the patient enters the screening age range, develops new breast symptoms or identifies hereditary risk.
management.safety: Never call a symptomatic breast lump 'screening'; it requires diagnostic assessment.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 44-year-old notices a changing 9 mm pigmented back lesion with asymmetric borders, colour variegation and a new nodular component. His mother had melanoma. There is no infection or bleeding.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Perform punch biopsy of only the darkest area without assessing full thickness.
Arrange urgent dermatology review but avoid biopsy until pigment changes stop.
Arrange a complete excisional biopsy of the suspicious pigmented lesion.
Apply cryotherapy as a trial and excise only if the lesion recurs.
Obtain PET-CT for staging before any tissue diagnosis of the primary lesion.
explanations: A partial punch sample can miss the thickest component and underestimate Breslow depth in a small excisable lesion. Complete excision with narrow margins is generally preferred for suspicious melanoma.
Dermatology review is appropriate, but a changing asymmetric pigmented lesion with nodularity requires prompt tissue diagnosis, not observation for regression.

Correct: changing ABCDE features require histopathologic diagnosis with accurate Breslow staging. Clinical distinction: Evolution, asymmetry, border irregularity and colour variation are high-risk melanoma signs; histology determines staging.
Cryotherapy destroys architecture needed for histological diagnosis and may delay melanoma recognition. Excisional biopsy is needed for staging and management planning.
Systemic staging imaging is not the initial step for an undiagnosed localised suspicious lesion. Histology and Breslow thickness determine subsequent staging needs.
pearl: Evolution, asymmetry, border irregularity and colour variation are high-risk melanoma signs; histology determines staging.
pivot: A stable symmetric uniformly coloured nevus without concerning features may be photographed/monitored under appropriate dermoscopy review.

steps: Arrange a complete excisional biopsy of the suspicious pigmented lesion.
Excisional biopsy with narrow diagnostic margins when feasible, or dermatology referral for complex sites.
Histological Breslow thickness and ulceration guide wider excision and sentinel node discussion.
Sun protection and skin surveillance for patient/family.
management.safety: Do not destroy suspicious lesions without histology.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 32-year-old ten days after Caesarean delivery develops sudden pleuritic pain, severe breathlessness and collapse. HR 138/min, BP 72/40 mmHg, SpO2 84% and the right ventricle is severely dilated on bedside echocardiography. There is no major bleeding currently.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate immediate approach?
options: Arrange urgent CTPA before any reperfusion discussion despite profound shock.
Give therapeutic anticoagulation alone and wait for haemodynamic improvement.
Administer large repeated fluid boluses without monitoring right-heart strain.
Resuscitate and assess urgently for PE reperfusion after Caesarean delivery.
Give prophylactic LMWH and arrange formal echocardiography the next morning.
explanations: CTPA is definitive when feasible, but BP 72/40, severe hypoxia and RV dilation demand immediate resuscitation and multidisciplinary high-risk PE evaluation. Imaging must not delay a lifesaving intervention in an unstable patient.

Anticoagulation is important, yet shock from likely massive PE often requires consideration of urgent reperfusion. Recent Caesarean substantially raises bleeding risk, so select thrombolysis, catheter or surgery through senior multidisciplinary assessment.
Excessive crystalloid can overdistend a failing right ventricle and reduce cardiac output. Give fluids cautiously only when indicated while arranging vasopressors and definitive PE treatment.

Correct: obstructive shock with high-probability PE needs ABC support and urgent specialist reperfusion consideration. Clinical distinction: Postpartum PE can present as obstructive shock; a normal or modest D-dimer is not a safe exclusion test in this setting.

Prophylactic anticoagulation is inadequate for suspected life-threatening PE, and waiting overnight would be dangerous. Start appropriate high-acuity treatment with obstetric, critical-care and PE specialists.
pearl: Postpartum PE can present as obstructive shock; a normal or modest D-dimer is not a safe exclusion test in this setting.
pivot: If stable with lower probability, use an appropriate structured diagnostic pathway and definitive imaging rather than emergency reperfusion.

steps: Resuscitate and assess urgently for PE reperfusion after Caesarean delivery.
Carefully assess fluid response; use vasopressors as required for persistent hypotension and avoid unnecessary transfer.

Urgent CTPA if stable for imaging; if too unstable, multidisciplinary decision based on bedside findings and probability; anticoagulation and reperfusion according to bleeding risk and service availability.
Monitor haemorrhage and haemodynamics, assess provoking factors, counsel on anticoagulation compatible with breastfeeding under specialist advice.
management.safety: Recent surgery and postpartum haemorrhage risks materially affect choice of thrombolysis versus catheter/surgical alternatives.
management.local: Educational sequence only: verify drug doses, contraindications and escalation pathways with your current local protocol and supervising clinician.

stem: A 2-year-old has a barking cough and inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate intercostal recession and agitation. He is pink with SpO2 96%, is speaking in short phrases, and no choking event occurred.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give oral dexamethasone alone and discharge while stridor persists at rest.
Give dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline, with monitored observation.
Administer nebulised salbutamol as first-line for inspiratory upper-airway noise.
Intubate immediately despite preserved oxygenation and no exhaustion signs.
Give nebulised adrenaline but omit corticosteroid and discharge once calmer.
explanations: Dexamethasone is important, but stridor at rest with moderate recession indicates more severe croup requiring nebulised adrenaline and observation for recurrence after its short effect wears off.

Correct: stridor at rest indicates moderate/severe croup requiring corticosteroid and inhaled adrenaline with observation. Clinical distinction: Croup is upper-airway oedema: dexamethasone provides sustained benefit; nebulised adrenaline gives rapid but temporary relief.
Salbutamol acts on lower-airway bronchospasm and does not reliably relieve the subglottic swelling causing croup stridor. Nebulised adrenaline and steroid target the correct pathology.

Intubation is reserved for severe impending airway failure, exhaustion or deterioration despite treatment. This child can still vocalise and oxygenate, so medical therapy with close assessment is appropriate initially.
Adrenaline provides rapid temporary relief but does not replace the longer anti-inflammatory benefit of dexamethasone. Observation is needed as adrenaline wears off.
pearl: Croup is upper-airway oedema: dexamethasone provides sustained benefit; nebulised adrenaline gives rapid but temporary relief.
pivot: If drooling, toxic appearance, tripod posture or difficult swallowing dominate, consider epiglottitis/deep neck infection and call expert airway help.

steps: Give dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline, with monitored observation.
Give dexamethasone per local croup protocol and nebulised adrenaline when stridor at rest or significant respiratory distress.
Observe after adrenaline for recurrence; seek senior/anaesthetic support for exhaustion, cyanosis, reduced consciousness or poor response.
management.safety: Do not perform throat examination that agitates a child with suspected dangerous upper-airway obstruction.
management.local: Use current maternity/paediatric local protocols, weight-based prescribing checks and senior supervision for doses and timing.

stem: A 46-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis and immunosuppressive therapy has a hot swollen knee, fever 38.6 °C and cannot bear weight. BP 120/70 mmHg. Bedside ultrasound shows a large effusion.
ask: What is the BEST initial approach?
options: Aspirate the joint before antibiotics if safe, then treat septic arthritis.
Begin empiric IV antibiotics before any cultures despite current haemodynamic stability.
Treat as rheumatoid flare with systemic steroids while arranging next-week review.
Order MRI of the knee before performing diagnostic joint aspiration.
Start oral NSAIDs first and aspirate only if fever persists after two days.
explanations: Correct: aspiration confirms infection and guides microbiology, while prompt antibiotics and source control protect joint and patient. Clinical distinction: Septic arthritis is a joint emergency: aspiration before antibiotics is ideal if stable, but do not delay antimicrobials in sepsis.

Antibiotics should not be delayed if septic or unstable, but a stable patient with a readily accessible hot joint should undergo prompt aspiration and blood cultures to optimise microbiology before treatment.
RA and immunosuppression increase septic-arthritis risk. Steroids could worsen an infected joint, and inability to weight bear with fever needs same-day investigation and treatment.
MRI can help evaluate osteomyelitis or complex anatomy, but should not delay a diagnostic aspirate from a clear effusion. Synovial fluid cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals are key.
NSAIDs may relieve pain, but do not eradicate a rapidly destructive joint infection. Prompt aspiration and empirical IV antibiotics after cultures are time-critical.
pearl: Septic arthritis is a joint emergency: aspiration before antibiotics is ideal if stable, but do not delay antimicrobials in sepsis.
pivot: If haemodynamically unstable, start antibiotics immediately after feasible cultures without waiting for aspiration.

steps: Aspirate the joint before antibiotics if safe, then treat septic arthritis.
Aseptic joint aspirate for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals; crystals do not exclude concurrent infection.
Empiric IV antibiotics guided by local resistance and risk factors; urgent washout/drainage as required.
Tailor therapy to culture, repeat assessment for ongoing infection and rehabilitation when safe.
management.safety: Immunosuppression can blunt fever or inflammatory signs; maintain a low threshold for septic arthritis.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 43-year-old with obesity presents with tiredness and thirst. HbA1c is 82 mmol/mol (9.7%) and fasting glucose 13 mmol/L. He is not acidotic, has no ketones or catabolic weight loss, and renal function is normal.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Begin diabetes pharmacotherapy with lifestyle care and early follow-up.
Start lifestyle changes only and repeat HbA1c after six months without medication.
Commence routine IV insulin infusion because HbA1c is above 9% despite no DKA.
Treat as probable autoimmune diabetes solely from the report of thirst.
Use basal insulin alone permanently without discussing other first-line agents.
explanations: Correct: significant hyperglycaemia needs a structured treatment plan, not lifestyle advice alone; drug choice is individualised. Clinical distinction: New type 2 diabetes management includes lifestyle, individualised glucose-lowering drugs, cardiovascular/renal risk and retinal/foot screening.

With marked symptomatic hyperglycaemia, lifestyle intervention remains essential but delaying pharmacotherapy for months is unlikely to achieve safe control. Discuss appropriate medication, usually including metformin if suitable.
IV insulin is indicated for acute decompensation such as DKA/HHS, not automatically for an ambulant non-ketotic patient with high HbA1c. Individualised oral or injectable therapy is more suitable.
Polyuria or thirst occur in type 2 as well as type 1 diabetes. If clinical features suggest autoimmune disease, investigate, but age, obesity and absence of ketosis do not establish type 1.

Insulin may be appropriate if symptomatic severe hyperglycaemia or other factors require it, but it is not invariably the sole lifelong therapy. Select treatment by phenotype, comorbidities, glucose and patient preferences.
pearl: New type 2 diabetes management includes lifestyle, individualised glucose-lowering drugs, cardiovascular/renal risk and retinal/foot screening.
pivot: Marked ketosis, rapid weight loss, dehydration or acidosis raises concern for insulin deficiency/DKA and changes urgency.

steps: Begin diabetes pharmacotherapy with lifestyle care and early follow-up.
Diet/activity support and pharmacotherapy, commonly metformin if suitable; consider early combination or insulin for very high symptomatic glucose, guided by comorbidities.
Home glucose review, adherence, education and hypoglycaemia safety when applicable; titrate treatment within weeks.
Discuss smoking cessation, vaccinations, BP/lipids and kidney/cardiovascular protective agents when indicated.
management.safety: Do not start metformin in significant metabolic acidosis or unstable renal failure; selection depends on eGFR and risk.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 59-year-old woman with recurrent calcium oxalate renal stones has corrected calcium 2.86 mmol/L and an inappropriately elevated PTH. Renal function is stable and she has no severe dehydration.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate long-term management discussion?
options: Begin bisphosphonate therapy as definitive treatment of the parathyroid disease.
Order repeat thyroid ultrasound because recurrent stones imply thyroid dysfunction.
Recommend observation alone despite symptomatic recurrent nephrolithiasis.
Discuss definitive parathyroidectomy given recurrent renal stones from symptomatic hyperparathyroidism.
Give regular phosphate supplementation as a permanent curative strategy.
explanations: Antiresorptive medicines may improve bone density or calcium in selected patients unable to have surgery but do not remove the source of excess PTH. Recurrent stones are an indication to discuss parathyroidectomy.
An inappropriately raised PTH in hypercalcaemia points toward parathyroid rather than thyroid hormone pathology. Assessment includes biochemical confirmation and specialist surgical criteria.
Surveillance may suit selected asymptomatic patients, but recurrent calcium stones demonstrate symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism and favour discussion of definitive surgery.

Correct: nephrolithiasis with biochemistry of primary hyperparathyroidism is a reason to discuss surgery. Clinical distinction: Kidney stones, fractures/osteoporosis and other organ complications support surgical management of primary hyperparathyroidism.
Phosphate is not the standard long-term cure for autonomous parathyroid disease and can introduce mineral-balance complications. Surgical assessment is indicated in symptomatic disease.
pearl: Kidney stones, fractures/osteoporosis and other organ complications support surgical management of primary hyperparathyroidism.
pivot: In frail asymptomatic patients not meeting surgical criteria, surveillance and medical risk management may be chosen.

steps: Discuss definitive parathyroidectomy given recurrent renal stones from symptomatic hyperparathyroidism.
Bone density, renal imaging for stones and eGFR; differentiate familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia.
Endocrine surgery discussion for symptomatic disease; localisation imaging is for operative planning, not diagnosis.
Hydration counselling and calcium/bone/renal follow-up if surgery deferred.
management.safety: Avoid diagnosing adenoma solely on neck ultrasound without biochemical confirmation.
management.local: Educational guidance; check current hospital guidelines, prescribing references and senior advice for exact treatment details.

stem: A 25-year-old had suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole six weeks ago. Initial hCG declined but has now plateaued across several weekly samples. She feels well and pelvic ultrasound shows no retained tissue.
ask: What is the NEXT best step?
options: Repeat uterine evacuation immediately as the first response to any hCG plateau.
Assume persistent low hCG is normal and reduce monitoring to annual review.
Give empiric methotrexate before specialist staging or diagnostic criteria review.
Refer urgently to the GTD centre for assessment of persistent post-molar hCG.
Obtain a single repeat hCG in six months and reassess if bleeding occurs.
explanations: Repeat curettage may be considered for selected persistent disease under specialist care, but indiscriminate re-evacuation risks uterine injury and may not treat extrauterine gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
Serial hCG plateau after molar evacuation is concerning for post-molar GTN despite a normal ultrasound. Stopping surveillance can miss treatable persistent disease.
Chemotherapy may be appropriate after specialist diagnosis and staging, but should not be started blindly without assessing hCG kinetics, metastatic risk and recommended risk scoring.

Correct: plateauing hCG after molar pregnancy may meet criteria for persistent GTN. Clinical distinction: Serial hCG trajectory, not symptoms or ultrasound alone, determines persistent post-molar disease concern.
An hCG plateau over serial weekly values triggers prompt GTD-centre review rather than prolonged delay. Early risk stratification guides highly effective treatment.
pearl: Serial hCG trajectory, not symptoms or ultrasound alone, determines persistent post-molar disease concern.
pivot: A consistently declining hCG within protocol-defined timelines is managed with continued surveillance rather than immediate chemotherapy.

steps: Refer urgently to the GTD centre for assessment of persistent post-molar hCG.
Specialist GTD service; pelvic and metastatic assessment as indicated, FIGO risk scoring.
Risk-adapted chemotherapy or selected alternatives under GTD centre; continue hCG surveillance.
Reliable contraception during monitoring and support for future pregnancy planning.
management.safety: Future pregnancy should generally wait until specialised follow-up is complete.
management.local: Exam-oriented summary: confirm exact obstetric medication, fetal monitoring and delivery thresholds with the local maternity pathway.

skill: Failure to thrive / social & organic assessment
stem: A 9-month-old has dropped from the 50th to below the 3rd weight centile over five months. Development is mildly delayed, there is chronic watery diarrhoea and abdominal distension. Parents report frequent feeding but no blood in stools.
ask: Which initial evaluation is MOST appropriate?
options: Begin a high-calorie diet immediately without assessing the cause of faltering growth.
Order coeliac serology alone and ignore feeding, growth and psychosocial history.
Review growth, feeding, social context and causes of malabsorption.
Diagnose neglect on the weight graph alone and begin legal action before examination.
Prescribe empirical steroids for inflammatory bowel disease without investigations.
explanations: Nutritional support is often needed, but profound centile crossing with chronic diarrhoea and distension warrants a comprehensive feeding, developmental and medical assessment. Supplements alone may miss malabsorption.
Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive causes warrant consideration, but no single test replaces accurate anthropometry, dietary history, developmental, family and social assessment.

Correct: faltering growth with diarrhoea warrants measured intake, examination and targeted investigation. Clinical distinction: Faltering growth is a pattern, not a single low weight; look at trajectory, intake, symptoms, development and family context.

Safeguarding should be considered sensitively when indicated, but weight faltering has many organic and non-organic causes. A balanced history, examination and multidisciplinary evaluation come first.
Empirical immunosuppression without diagnosis risks harm and can mask infection. Initial testing should be driven by growth pattern and symptoms before specialist treatment.
pearl: Faltering growth is a pattern, not a single low weight; look at trajectory, intake, symptoms, development and family context.
pivot: A constitutionally small but consistently tracking child with normal development may require reassurance rather than broad tests.

steps: Review growth, feeding, social context and causes of malabsorption.
Feeding observation, diet history, stool pattern, developmental and family/social history, full exam.
FBC, iron, coeliac testing when gluten-exposed, stool studies or endocrine workup based on findings.
Dietitian/paediatric referral, safe energy improvement and timed repeat measurements.
management.safety: Always screen for dehydration and nutritional deficiencies; avoid assuming blame.
management.local: Paediatric doses, age thresholds and neonatal algorithms must be checked against local protocols and senior paediatric advice.

stem: A 17-year-old has sudden severe left testicular pain for four hours, vomiting, a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex. No dysuria, fever or trauma. Surgical help is immediately available.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Operate urgently for likely testicular torsion without waiting for ultrasound.
Obtain scrotal Doppler before involving urology even though theatre is available.
Attempt prolonged manual detorsion in ED and defer surgical fixation if pain improves.
Start IV antibiotics for epididymo-orchitis and reassess after analgesia.
Arrange observation for six hours to distinguish intermittent torsion from trauma.
explanations: Correct: salvage falls with time, and contralateral fixation is usually performed. Clinical distinction: Testicular torsion is a clinical time emergency; prompt surgical exploration outranks Doppler when suspicion is high.
Doppler can aid equivocal cases, but a classic acute torsion presentation requires immediate urological exploration. Imaging must not delay detorsion in a four-hour time-sensitive window.
Manual detorsion may be an interim measure if surgery is delayed but does not replace exploration and bilateral orchidopexy. Residual torsion can persist despite symptom relief.
Epididymitis usually has a less abrupt onset and may have urinary/infectious symptoms. Sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding transverse testis and absent reflex favour torsion.
Observation risks ischaemic loss of the testis. Clinical suspicion with immediate surgical availability warrants urgent exploration.
pearl: Testicular torsion is a clinical time emergency; prompt surgical exploration outranks Doppler when suspicion is high.
pivot: Gradual scrotal pain with urinary symptoms and preserved cremasteric reflex may suggest epididymitis, though torsion must still be excluded.

steps: Operate urgently for likely testicular torsion without waiting for ultrasound.
Urgent urology/theatre, do not delay for Doppler if high suspicion.
Surgical detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy when viable; orchidectomy if nonviable.
Fertility risk and prompt return for contralateral or recurrent pain.
management.safety: Manual detorsion by trained staff may buy time but must not replace operative exploration.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 46-year-old after a fall has mild head injury and is repeatedly asking the same questions. He insists on leaving ED while vomiting twice and cannot explain the danger of intracranial bleeding. GCS is 14.
ask: Which response is MOST appropriate?
options: Use next-of-kin consent alone without assessing the patient's actual capacity.
Let him leave because verbal refusal always establishes valid informed consent.
Assess decision-making capacity and use emergency care authority if needed.
Give prophylactic sedatives and physically restrain him until tomorrow's round.
Arrange outpatient CT after discharge if the patient later agrees to imaging.
explanations: Family can provide collateral information and support, but a relative's signature does not substitute for capacity assessment or the applicable legal process. The patient may be unable to understand or weigh acute risks.
Capacity is decision-specific, not a simple ability to say 'no'. Repetitive questions, vomiting and inability to explain possible intracranial injury raise serious concerns about informed refusal.

Correct: memory impairment may undermine appreciation of immediate risk; prioritise safety within local law. Clinical distinction: Capacity is decision- and time-specific, not equivalent to orientation or GCS alone.
Any restriction must be clinically and legally justified, proportionate, monitored and least restrictive. Indefinite restraint without a capacity and emergency-risk evaluation is inappropriate.
Repeated vomiting, GCS 14 and post-traumatic confusion warrant immediate head-injury evaluation. Deferring imaging to routine outpatient review may miss intracranial haemorrhage.
pearl: Capacity is decision- and time-specific, not equivalent to orientation or GCS alone.
pivot: A patient who accurately understands and weighs risks may retain capacity even when declining clinician advice.

steps: Assess decision-making capacity and use emergency care authority if needed.
Manage pain, nausea and possible intoxication; obtain CT/head injury assessment as required.
If lacks capacity and serious imminent harm, use legally authorised least-restrictive emergency care.
Specific deficits, rationale, actions and reassessment.
management.safety: Never equate an unwise decision with incapacity.
management.local: Follow local mental health, safeguarding and prescribing policy; exact doses and legal requirements vary.

stem: A 73-year-old with benign prostatic hyperplasia has suprapubic discomfort and minimal urine for 18 hours. Creatinine is 220 µmol/L (baseline 95), bladder scan shows 1100 mL, and ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. He is stable without sepsis.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange elective cystoscopy before draining the bladder because he is stable.
Catheterise the bladder and monitor for post-obstructive diuresis.
Give IV fluids and diuretics to stimulate flow without relieving retention.
Start an alpha blocker and reassess urine output after 48 hours.
Begin dialysis for acute kidney injury before attempting urinary drainage.
explanations: Aetiological investigation such as cystoscopy can follow stabilisation, but 1100 mL retention with bilateral hydronephrosis and AKI needs prompt bladder drainage.

Correct: mechanical bladder outlet obstruction causes postrenal AKI; drainage and surveillance are essential. Clinical distinction: Postrenal AKI may improve after drainage, but brisk post-obstructive diuresis can cause fluid/electrolyte loss.
Diuretics do not relieve a mechanical bladder-outlet obstruction, and excess fluid can worsen pressure. Drain with a catheter, monitor electrolytes and urine output afterward.
Alpha blockers can facilitate later trial without catheter, but will not rapidly relieve severe retention and renal obstruction. Immediate decompression is indicated.
Dialysis may be needed for refractory complications but the reversible cause here is obstruction. Catheterisation and monitoring for post-obstructive diuresis take priority.
pearl: Postrenal AKI may improve after drainage, but brisk post-obstructive diuresis can cause fluid/electrolyte loss.
pivot: In painless chronic retention without renal impairment, urgency and approach may differ but still need urologic assessment.

steps: Catheterise the bladder and monitor for post-obstructive diuresis.
Hourly urine output initially, BP, Na/K/creatinine and fluid balance for post-obstructive diuresis.
Review alpha blockade, prostate evaluation and long-term catheter/operative options.
Look for sepsis, haematuria or failure of creatinine recovery.
management.safety: Avoid repeated traumatic catheter attempts if urethral injury is suspected.
management.local: Educational answer; confirm local clinical guidelines, doses and relevant senior-led escalation.

stem: A 25-year-old after a motorcycle collision is agitated, severely hypoxic and hypotensive. There are absent left breath sounds, hyperresonance and progressive neck-vein distension. Tracheal position is difficult to assess.
ask: What should happen FIRST?
options: Give a crystalloid bolus and reassess before treating the unilateral chest signs.
Perform immediate left thoracic decompression followed by definitive pleural drainage and resuscitation.
Arrange a portable chest radiograph before emergency thoracic intervention.
Intubate and increase ventilator pressure to improve oxygenation first.
Perform ultrasound only and await confirmation before any decompression.
explanations: Resuscitation may include fluid or blood depending on trauma, but classic tension physiology with hypoxia, hypotension and absent unilateral sounds requires immediate decompression. Boluses cannot reverse obstructive shock.

Correct: classic unilateral signs with shock mandate immediate decompression before radiography. Clinical distinction: In shock with unilateral absent breath sounds after trauma, treat suspected tension pneumothorax immediately; do not await tracheal deviation.
Imaging is not needed to treat suspected tension pneumothorax in a haemodynamically unstable trauma patient. Waiting risks cardiac arrest.
Positive-pressure ventilation before releasing intrathoracic pressure can worsen the tension and precipitate arrest. Decompress immediately while providing airway support as necessary.
Ultrasound can support rapid diagnosis if immediately available, but should not delay treatment when clinical signs are compelling. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical emergency.
pearl: In shock with unilateral absent breath sounds after trauma, treat suspected tension pneumothorax immediately; do not await tracheal deviation.
pivot: A stable simple pneumothorax can be assessed radiologically and treated according to size, symptoms and risk factors.

steps: Perform immediate left thoracic decompression followed by definitive pleural drainage and resuscitation.
Perform immediate finger thoracostomy or needle decompression at locally approved site/technique based on skills and environment.
Insert intercostal drain and confirm lung re-expansion; search for associated injuries.
Repeat breath sounds, SpO2 and haemodynamics; review imaging after decompression when safe.
management.safety: Treat before positive-pressure ventilation if possible; emergency decompression technique/site varies with trauma protocol and expertise.
management.local: Educational sequence only: verify drug doses, contraindications and escalation pathways with your current local protocol and supervising clinician.

stem: A 12-day-old infant has a measured temperature of 38.3 °C at home and poor feeding. He is now afebrile in ED after paracetamol, interactive but slightly mottled. Birth and maternal history were uncomplicated.
ask: Which is the BEST initial approach?
options: Admit for neonatal sepsis assessment and empirical IV antibiotics.
Collect only a urine sample and discharge if its screening dipstick is normal.
Perform viral testing first, reserving cultures for a negative respiratory panel.
Observe for recurrence of fever because paracetamol has normalised temperature.
Treat poor feeding with supplemental formula and arrange GP review tomorrow.
explanations: Correct: in a 12-day-old with documented fever, evaluate blood/urine/CSF and treat serious bacterial infection without unsafe delay. Clinical distinction: Young febrile neonates need a low threshold for blood, urine and CSF assessment plus empiric IV treatment, even if afebrile at review.

Young neonates with documented fever need a systematic invasive bacterial infection assessment, typically including blood, urine and CSF as clinically appropriate. A normal urine screen cannot exclude bacteraemia or meningitis.
Viral infection does not exclude concurrent serious bacterial disease in a twelve-day-old. Diagnostic work-up and empiric IV antibiotics should not await a respiratory panel.
Antipyretic response does not remove the significance of an accurately measured fever in an infant under one month, especially with poor feeding and mottling.
Feeding support is important but does not address the possibility of rapidly progressive neonatal sepsis. Hospital assessment, monitoring and empiric therapy are indicated.
pearl: Young febrile neonates need a low threshold for blood, urine and CSF assessment plus empiric IV treatment, even if afebrile at review.
pivot: An older well-appearing infant may be eligible for a risk-stratified testing and observation pathway depending on corrected age and local guidance.

steps: Admit for neonatal sepsis assessment and empirical IV antibiotics.
FBC, inflammatory markers, blood culture, catheter/SPA urine culture and lumbar puncture if safe; consider HSV testing/treatment if clinically indicated.
Give empiric IV antibiotics promptly after feasible cultures; do not delay for difficult LP or reassuring viral tests.
Admit for serial clinical review, fluid and glucose support, culture follow-up and antibiotic adjustment.
management.safety: Meningitis signs are often subtle in neonates; normal behaviour at one time point is not reliable exclusion.
management.local: Use current maternity/paediatric local protocols, weight-based prescribing checks and senior supervision for doses and timing.

stem: A 49-year-old with a history of lumbar disc prolapse reports new urinary retention, bilateral sciatica, reduced perineal sensation and progressive foot weakness. Post-void residual is 800 mL.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Catheterise for retention and reassess saddle sensation after analgesia.
Arrange outpatient physiotherapy because lumbar disc symptoms often improve.
Obtain urgent spinal MRI and surgical input for suspected cauda equina.
Perform nerve-conduction tests before considering spinal decompression.
Give high-dose steroids alone and arrange repeat bladder scan next week.
explanations: Bladder drainage treats retention but does not relieve cauda equina compression. New saddle sensory loss, bilateral sciatica and progressive weakness need emergent MRI and surgical review.
Conservative treatment is appropriate for many uncomplicated disc prolapses, but cauda equina red flags demand immediate evaluation. Delay can cause permanent bladder, bowel and motor deficits.

Correct: suspected cauda equina syndrome requires same-day imaging and assessment for urgent decompression. Clinical distinction: New urinary dysfunction plus saddle change with back pain is an emergency even if limb power and rectal tone are partly preserved.
Electrodiagnostic testing is not the time-critical investigation for suspected cauda equina syndrome. MRI identifies a compressive lesion and guides decompression.
Steroids may have roles in other spinal emergencies but are not definitive treatment for disc-related cauda equina compression. Urgent surgery may be required.
pearl: New urinary dysfunction plus saddle change with back pain is an emergency even if limb power and rectal tone are partly preserved.
pivot: For uncomplicated mechanical radicular pain without bladder/saddle red flags, analgesia, activity and conservative follow-up may be appropriate.

steps: Obtain urgent spinal MRI and surgical input for suspected cauda equina.
Emergency MRI lumbar spine; do not let delays in routine investigation or analgesia mask evolving deficits.
Bladder catheter if retention, analgesia and prepare for urgent surgical decompression if compression confirmed.
Careful timing of symptom onset, serial neurological examination and informed consent.
management.safety: A missed cauda equina syndrome can lead to permanent bowel, bladder and sexual dysfunction.
management.local: Study framework only: medication selection and operative decisions follow current hospital protocols and responsible specialist advice.

stem: A 59-year-old at day nine after chemotherapy for lymphoma has temperature 38.7 °C, rigors and ANC 0.2 × 10^9/L. BP 103/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96%. He has a central venous catheter and no focal symptoms.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Obtain central and peripheral cultures, then wait for growth before treatment.
Give colony-stimulating factor alone until neutrophils recover spontaneously.
Start a narrow oral antibiotic while observing on a general ward.
Remove the central line before administering any antibacterial therapy.
Give immediate broad-spectrum IV antipseudomonal antibiotics.
explanations: Blood cultures should be taken rapidly if they will not delay care, but febrile profound neutropenia is a medical emergency. Waiting for growth risks sepsis and death.
G-CSF is sometimes considered in selected situations but does not treat an established potentially invasive infection. Immediate broad IV antimicrobial coverage is required.
Oral treatment can suit carefully selected low-risk febrile neutropenia. ANC 0.2, rigors, central line and recent chemotherapy warrant urgent IV antipseudomonal therapy and monitoring.
Line infection requires evaluation and possible removal, but empiric antibiotics should not be delayed for catheter procedures. Obtain appropriate cultures and reassess the device based on findings.

Correct: febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency even without shock or a clear source. Clinical distinction: Fever after chemotherapy with profound neutropenia is presumptive infection until proven otherwise; normal blood pressure does not justify delay.
pearl: Fever after chemotherapy with profound neutropenia is presumptive infection until proven otherwise; normal blood pressure does not justify delay.
pivot: A stable low-risk neutropenic patient may be considered for selected oral/outpatient pathways after structured risk assessment and specialist input.

steps: Give immediate broad-spectrum IV antipseudomonal antibiotics.
Blood cultures from peripheral and each central line lumen as appropriate, FBC, renal/liver function, lactate and focused source tests.
Begin IV broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antibiotic promptly per hospital neutropenic fever protocol; add coverage based on instability/resistance.
Frequent vital signs, culture adjustment, review for invasive fungal disease if fever persists, haemodynamic escalation when needed.
management.safety: Avoid routine rectal examination and delaying antibiotics for imaging.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 24-year-old at 19 weeks gestation develops fever 39.1 °C, dysuria, left costovertebral angle tenderness and vomiting. BP is 112/68 mmHg and fetal heartbeat is normal. Urine dip has nitrites and leukocytes.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate treatment plan?
options: Start oral nitrofurantoin because it concentrates in urine despite flank pain.
Arrange renal ultrasonography and delay antibiotics until obstruction is excluded.
Give a single intramuscular antibiotic dose and discharge if vomiting stops.
Admit for IV treatment and monitoring of pyelonephritis in pregnancy.
Treat with a short oral beta-lactam course alone and review at the next visit.
explanations: Nitrofurantoin is useful for lower UTI but does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal levels to treat pyelonephritis. Pregnancy with fever, flank pain and vomiting warrants IV therapy.
Imaging can identify obstruction or complications in selected cases, but it must not delay empiric antibiotics for likely upper urinary tract infection in pregnancy.
Vomiting and systemic fever place her at risk of dehydration, bacteraemia and obstetric complications; a single injection without observation is insufficient.

Correct: febrile upper UTI in pregnancy warrants parenteral therapy and assessment for sepsis and preterm contractions. Clinical distinction: Pregnancy changes UTI management: pyelonephritis risks maternal sepsis, ARDS and preterm birth, so admission and IV therapy are appropriate.
Oral step-down therapy can follow clinical improvement, but initial admission and IV antibiotics are commonly recommended for pyelonephritis in pregnancy.
pearl: Pregnancy changes UTI management: pyelonephritis risks maternal sepsis, ARDS and preterm birth, so admission and IV therapy are appropriate.
pivot: An asymptomatic bacteriuria diagnosis in pregnancy still warrants targeted treatment but without the same emergency inpatient bundle.

steps: Admit for IV treatment and monitoring of pyelonephritis in pregnancy.
Prompt pregnancy-compatible IV beta-lactam-based antibiotics per local microbiology, fluids and antiemetics.
Temperature, flank pain, urine output, renal function and culture sensitivities; investigate obstruction if poor response.
Step down to oral antibiotics once clinically improving, complete treatment and plan follow-up urine testing.
management.safety: Avoid drugs with fetal risk or poor renal tissue penetration; consider resistant pathogens and allergy.
management.local: Educational guidance; check current hospital guidelines, prescribing references and senior advice for exact treatment details.

stem: A 57-year-old postmenopausal woman with obesity presents with recurrent painless vaginal spotting for two months. She is not taking hormone therapy. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrial thickness of 12 mm.
ask: Which investigation is MOST appropriate?
options: Repeat ultrasound in six months because obesity can thicken the endometrium.
Arrange prompt endometrial biopsy to exclude hyperplasia or malignancy in postmenopausal bleeding.
Offer progestogen therapy without excluding atypia or malignancy first.
Order serum CA125 before deciding whether endometrial biopsy is necessary.
Treat presumed vaginal atrophy and review only if bleeding becomes heavy.
explanations: Recurrent postmenopausal bleeding with a 12 mm endometrium requires tissue assessment. Observation alone may miss hyperplasia or endometrial cancer.

Correct: tissue diagnosis is necessary to rule out hyperplasia or malignancy. Clinical distinction: Postmenopausal bleeding requires assessment for endometrial cancer; endometrial thickness guides testing but symptoms remain key.
Progestogen treatment may be appropriate for certain confirmed hyperplasia types but should not be prescribed blindly without histological assessment of a thickened endometrium.
CA125 is not an initial diagnostic replacement for endometrial sampling. Tissue diagnosis is necessary to assess hyperplasia and malignancy risk.
Atrophy is common, but it should not be assumed when bleeding recurs with endometrial thickening and obesity. Malignancy must be excluded.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding requires assessment for endometrial cancer; endometrial thickness guides testing but symptoms remain key.
pivot: If a single episode occurs with a thin endometrium at an accepted threshold, follow-up may be sufficient in selected low-risk women; persistent bleeding still requires evaluation.

steps: Arrange prompt endometrial biopsy to exclude hyperplasia or malignancy in postmenopausal bleeding.
Outpatient endometrial biopsy; hysteroscopy if technically difficult, persistent bleeding or focal lesion.
Gynaecology referral for atypical hyperplasia/cancer and specialist staging as appropriate.
Review persistent/recurrent bleeding even if earlier sample is benign.
management.safety: Do not dismiss repeated postmenopausal bleeding on the basis of a previous normal ultrasound.
management.local: Exam-oriented summary: confirm exact obstetric medication, fetal monitoring and delivery thresholds with the local maternity pathway.

stem: A 6-year-old with IgA vasculitis develops sudden severe intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting and a palpable mass in the right upper abdomen. She becomes pale during episodes. BP and urine output remain normal.
ask: Which complication requires urgent assessment?
options: Treat presumed vasculitis-related gut oedema and observe without imaging.
Begin corticosteroids alone for the abdominal pain before excluding obstruction.
Use oral rehydration only because renal observations are currently normal.
Arrange urgent CT abdomen as the routine first test in a stable child.
Assess urgently for intussusception with ultrasound and surgical input.
explanations: IgA vasculitis can cause bowel-wall oedema and pain, but episodic severe colic with pallor, vomiting and a palpable mass raises concern for intussusception requiring urgent imaging.
Corticosteroids may ease severe inflammatory pain in selected IgA vasculitis but cannot safely replace exclusion of intussusception or bowel compromise.
Normal renal parameters do not exclude a gastrointestinal emergency. The abdominal presentation needs prompt ultrasound and surgical assessment rather than hydration alone.
Ultrasound is the preferred first test for suspected intussusception in a stable child and avoids CT radiation. CT is reserved for uncertainty or complications.

Correct: intestinal vasculitic oedema can act as a lead point; ultrasound is appropriate. Clinical distinction: IgA vasculitis has GI complications including intussusception and bowel ischaemia, not only benign abdominal pain.
pearl: IgA vasculitis has GI complications including intussusception and bowel ischaemia, not only benign abdominal pain.
pivot: Mild abdominal discomfort without red flags may respond to supportive care and monitoring.

steps: Assess urgently for intussusception with ultrasound and surgical input.
Urgent ultrasound for intussusception and bowel involvement; assess for obstruction.
Paediatric surgery and senior paediatrics; IV support and reduction/surgery according to anatomy and viability.
BP and urinalysis over following months even if abdominal symptoms resolve.
management.safety: Severe pain, bilious vomiting or GI bleeding warrant emergency reassessment.
management.local: Paediatric doses, age thresholds and neonatal algorithms must be checked against local protocols and senior paediatric advice.

stem: A 69-year-old with AF develops sudden left leg pain and coldness. Left foot is pale, no Doppler arterial signals are heard, and she has new paraesthesia but can still move her toes. Onset was two hours ago.
ask: Which immediate management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give oral antiplatelet therapy and obtain outpatient vascular duplex next week.
Begin IV thrombolysis for the limb before contacting vascular surgery.
Elevate the leg and apply compression to improve arterial reperfusion.
Request diagnostic angiography tomorrow before starting anticoagulation.
Give IV heparin and arrange emergency vascular review for acute limb ischaemia.
explanations: Antiplatelets do not provide prompt anticoagulation or restore an acutely threatened limb. Absent arterial Doppler signals with paraesthesia require immediate vascular help.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis may be considered by a vascular team in selected patients, but systemic therapy without assessment is not the automatic first step. IV heparin and revascularisation planning are urgent.
Compression treats venous problems, not an acute arterial embolus. Elevating a critically ischaemic limb can reduce perfusion further.
Imaging can help plan treatment but should not delay heparin and emergency vascular consultation. Sensory changes suggest a threatened limb with little time to spare.

Correct: acute limb ischaemia needs rapid anticoagulation and definitive reperfusion planning. Clinical distinction: The 6 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia) help recognise acute limb ischaemia.
pearl: The 6 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia) help recognise acute limb ischaemia.
